To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a computer model of human passive thermoregulation can be used to predict human thermal responses to a wide range of environments and that the model predictions compare favorably with available data.

1) the passive system model can predict human thermal responses in a wide range of conditions, 2) the model can be used for both steady and transient conditions, 3) it can be applied to both sedentary and active conditions and to both clothed and unclothed individuals, and 4) the model can predict the effects of posture and activity on thermal response and comfort.
a model of the human thermal response can be formulated as a system of ordinary differential equations that can be solved numerically.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the human thermoregulatory system is highly complex, involving a large number of parameters, and that the modeling of heat transport in the body and at the periphery of the body is essential for the prediction of thermal comfort and the risk of heat stress.
